---
title: "Can I compare my samples?"
output: html_notebook
---

> Work through this notebook: run each chunk (click ▶). The full explanations
> and the **answers** to the "👉 Your turn" tasks are on the course website.

**The question:** before comparing conditions, are the samples themselves
comparable — or is one wildly different? The plot that answers it: the
**distribution of counts per sample**.

## Setup {-}

```{r setup03, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)   # here() builds paths from the project root, so they work wherever you run this
counts <- read_tsv(here("project/data", "gene_counts.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
meta   <- read_tsv(here("project/data", "metadata.tsv"),    show_col_types = FALSE)
```

First, reshape the counts to *tidy* form (one row per gene × sample) and attach the
sample info:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
counts_long <- counts %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(gene_id, gene_name), names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>%
  left_join(meta, by = "sample")

counts_long
```

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note — tidy (long) data:</strong> ggplot wants <em>one row per observation</em>.
  <code>pivot_longer()</code> turns the wide counts (a column per sample) into long form —
  one row per gene × sample — which is exactly what the geoms expect.
  <code>pivot_wider()</code> goes back the other way.
</div>

A boxplot per sample, coloured by lifestyle (counts are very skewed, so we plot them
on a log scale):

```{r, fig.height=6}
ggplot(counts_long, aes(x = sample, y = log10(count + 1), fill = lifestyle)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log10(count + 1)")
```

If the boxes line up at similar heights, the samples are comparable. 👍

**Why a boxplot here?** Each box summarises ~2,900 genes in one sample, so you can
compare all 32 samples at a glance — that's what a boxplot is good at: *comparing many
groups*. It doesn't show the *shape* of the distribution, though (the big spike of
low-count genes is hidden). To see the shape, a **density curve** is better — that's
your turn below. Same data, different question: boxplot = "do the samples line up?",
density = "what does one distribution look like?".

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Principle:</strong> match the plot to the question — a boxplot compares
  many groups compactly; a density curve shows the shape of one. (And skewed data like
  counts needs a log scale, or one huge value flattens everything else.)
</div>

::: question
<strong>🤔 Look closely.</strong> Do all 32 boxes sit at a similar height? If one is far
from the rest, that sample may be an outlier worth a second look before you trust any
comparison.
:::
